case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms-Burton Act creates jurisdiction to sue Cuban state agencies/instrumentalities for “trafficking” in expropriated property without requiring plaintiffs to plead and prove an applicable exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms-Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082, and the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611 (especially the presumption of immunity and the requirement of a statutory exception for jurisdiction).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Title III was enacted to provide an effective U.S. damages remedy for trafficking in property confiscated by the Castro regime and that Congress intended Title III actions to proceed against Cuban agencies and instrumentalities (such as CIMEX) without the additional hurdle of identifying and proving a separate FSIA exception. In Exxon’s view, Title III either (a) supplies its own jurisdiction/abrogation of immunity for covered defendants because it expressly authorizes suit against those who traffic (including Cuban state entities and their instrumentalities), or (b) should be read harmoniously with FSIA to avoid nullifying Title III’s core purpose—since the most relevant FSIA exceptions (e.g., expropriation/commercial-activity related exceptions) are difficult to satisfy in many Cuba trafficking cases. The United States, supporting Exxon, emphasizes foreign-policy interests in promoting accountability for Castro-era expropriations and compensating U.S. claimants through robust Title III enforcement.
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and the other respondents argue that FSIA is the exclusive basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so a Title III plaintiff must still satisfy an FSIA exception unless Congress clearly and explicitly displaced FSIA immunity—and Title III does not do so with the clarity required. Respondents contend that reading Title III to bypass FSIA would conflict with FSIA’s comprehensive framework, invite substantial diplomatic friction, and improperly subject foreign sovereign entities to U.S. litigation based on claims that necessarily challenge a sovereign’s public acts (the Cuban nationalizations). Respondents’ amici (foreign sovereign immunity and international law scholars/jurists) further argue that international practice recognizes concerns about suits that indirectly adjudicate or impair a foreign sovereign’s rights (sometimes described comparatively as “indirect impleading”), reinforcing the view that U.S. courts should require strict FSIA compliance before allowing Title III claims against state entities.
key_precedents: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act framework cases (general principle that FSIA provides the sole basis for jurisdiction over foreign sovereigns and their instrumentalities in U.S. courts)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s cause of action against “any person” who “traffics” would be significantly weakened if Cuban instrumentalities retain immunity, but that policy concern cannot substitute for the unmistakable clarity required to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive jurisdictional scheme. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence argument is persuasive: reading § 6082 as a silent carve-out would effectively amend §§ 1604–1605 by implication in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain where Congress knows how to speak clearly. Justice Alito’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Justice Thomas’s invocation of Verlinden reinforce that a cause of action does not itself supply jurisdiction over a foreign sovereign; FSIA and § 1330(a) remain the exclusive gateway absent an enumerated exception. Consistent with Helmerich & Payne, the narrow, institutionally legitimate resolution is that Title III does not alter FSIA, and plaintiffs must plausibly plead an FSIA exception (if one exists) at the threshold.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s cause of action against “any person” who “traffics” would be substantially weakened if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke immunity, but that policy concern cannot substitute for the clear statutory text required to displace the FSIA. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasized, Verlinden and Amerada Hess treat the FSIA as the sole basis for jurisdiction over foreign states, and Title III contains no unmistakable statement amending 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605 or otherwise withdrawing immunity. Justice Alito’s reminder that a cause of action is not itself a jurisdictional grant reinforces the textual point: § 6082 can coexist with FSIA by supplying liability rules only where an FSIA exception already opens the courthouse doors. Helmerich & Payne, as several colleagues noted, confirms that plaintiffs must plausibly plead an FSIA exception at the threshold, which forecloses treating Title III’s silence as an implied abrogation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially weakened if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke immunity, but that is a policy concern that cannot supply the unmistakable statement needed to displace the FSIA. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Verlinden and Amerada Hess is decisive for me: the FSIA is the exclusive gateway to jurisdiction over foreign states, and a remedial cause of action like § 6082 does not itself confer jurisdiction or abrogate immunity by implication. Justice Kagan is also right that reading § 6082 as a silent carve-out would effectively amend §§ 1604–1605 and fracture statutory coherence in a foreign-relations-sensitive area where Congress is expected to speak clearly. Helmerich & Payne, as Roberts and Sotomayor stress, reinforces the practical and jurisdictional necessity of requiring a plausibly pleaded FSIA exception at the outset rather than allowing Title III to do end-runs around immunity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s broad cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially narrowed if Cuban state instrumentalities can invoke immunity, but that kind of remedial-purpose inference cannot supply the unmistakable clarity needed to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Helmerich & Payne is especially persuasive to me: before a foreign sovereign (or its instrumentality) is subjected to the burdens of U.S. litigation, the plaintiff must make a legally sufficient, nonfrivolous showing that an FSIA exception applies, and Title III does not purport to alter that threshold jurisdictional rule. Justice Kagan and Justice Alito further reinforce the coherence point from Verlinden and Amerada Hess—FSIA is the sole gateway to jurisdiction, so reading § 6082’s silence as an implied abrogation would effectively amend §§ 1604–1605 by implication in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain. Even mindful of the statute’s justice-seeking aims for expropriation victims, our clear-statement doctrine and the FSIA’s exclusivity keep me with Respondent unless Congress expressly withdraws immunity or an enumerated FSIA exception is plausibly pleaded.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s cause of action against “any person” who “traffics” would be significantly narrowed if Cuban state entities can invoke immunity, but that functional concern cannot do the work of an unmistakable immunity withdrawal. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction (grounded in Verlinden and Amerada Hess) is the key coherence move: Title III can create liability rules while FSIA continues to gate access to court for sovereigns through its enumerated exceptions. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Helmerich & Payne strengthens the pragmatic, textual reading by reinforcing that an FSIA exception must be plausibly pleaded at the threshold to avoid imposing litigation burdens on sovereigns absent clear congressional authorization. On a careful textual analysis, § 6082’s silence about immunity is especially telling in a foreign-relations-sensitive area, so I would not infer an implied carve-out from FSIA.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be significantly undercut if Cuban instrumentalities may invoke immunity, but that is not a textual authorization to amend the FSIA by implication. Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement framing is decisive for me: in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain, Congress must speak unmistakably to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive rule of immunity, and 22 U.S.C. § 6082 nowhere does so. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Verlinden and Justice Kagan’s invocation of Amerada Hess reinforce that a cause of action does not itself confer jurisdiction over a sovereign; plaintiffs must still plead and prove an enumerated FSIA exception as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction. Helmerich & Payne, as Roberts emphasizes, further supports treating the FSIA exception inquiry as a threshold screen, which Title III’s silence cannot relax.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s cause of action against “any person” who “traffics” would be materially weakened if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke immunity, but that is not enough to displace the FSIA absent an unmistakable statement. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Verlinden and Amerada Hess is decisive for me: FSIA and § 1330(a) are the exclusive jurisdictional gateway, and a remedial cause of action does not itself create jurisdiction over a foreign state or its instrumentality. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence concern further reinforces that reading § 6082 as an implied carve-out would silently amend §§ 1604–1605 in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain where clear statements are required. Helmerich & Payne, as Roberts and Sotomayor note, underscores why we should insist on a plausibly pleaded FSIA exception at the threshold to avoid imposing litigation burdens on sovereigns.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Petitioner’s strongest point remains that Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” would be substantially undercut if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke immunity, but that functional concern cannot substitute for the clear statement required to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis that nothing in 22 U.S.C. § 6082 unmistakably abrogates immunity is decisive under a textualist approach, especially given Verlinden and Amerada Hess treating FSIA (via § 1330(a)) as the exclusive jurisdictional gateway. Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Helmerich & Payne further reinforces that an FSIA exception is a threshold jurisdictional prerequisite that must be plausibly alleged, which Title III’s silence cannot relax by implication. Harmonizing the statutes, Title III supplies a cause of action where jurisdiction exists, but it does not itself create jurisdiction over immune sovereign defendants absent an FSIA exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The petitioner’s strongest point—that Title III’s remedial design would be undercut if Cuban instrumentalities can invoke immunity—does not overcome our clear-statement requirement for withdrawing sovereign immunity, and § 6082 contains no unmistakable abrogation. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction, reinforced by Verlinden and Amerada Hess, fits my pragmatic concern for procedural fairness by preventing plaintiffs from using a broad cause of action to force jurisdictional fishing expeditions against foreign sovereign entities. Justice Kagan’s statutory-coherence point also matters: implying a Title III carve-out would silently rewrite FSIA’s calibrated exception structure in a foreign-relations-sensitive domain where Congress knows how to speak clearly. Helmerich & Payne, as Roberts and Sotomayor note, supports treating an FSIA exception as a plausibly pleaded threshold prerequisite, so Title III can supply a cause of action while FSIA still gates jurisdiction.

John Roberts.reasoning: FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, so a plaintiff must plead and ultimately establish a statutory exception to overcome the presumption of immunity. Nothing in Title III of the Helms-Burton Act, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, contains the clear statement necessary to displace FSIA’s comprehensive framework, and we should not infer a “blanket abrogation” in so sensitive an area of foreign relations. Under Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela v. Helmerich & Payne Int’l Drilling Co., whether an FSIA exception applies is a jurisdictional prerequisite that must be plausibly pleaded at the outset, particularly where the expropriation exception, 28 U.S.C. § 1605(a)(3), turns on whether the taking was “in violation of international law.” A narrow ruling preserving FSIA’s structure best respects precedent and institutional legitimacy while leaving any broader abrogation to Congress to state unmistakably.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “comprehensive set of legal standards governing claims of immunity in every civil action against a foreign state,” and it “provides the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” in our courts, so absent an applicable statutory exception a federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction. Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488 (1983); see also 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605; OBB Personenverkehr AG v. Sachs, 577 U.S. 27, 30 (2015). Nothing in Title III of Helms-Burton, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, contains a clear textual statement displacing the FSIA’s immunity framework for Cuban agencies and instrumentalities, and an express cause of action does not itself confer jurisdiction over immune sovereign defendants. Reading § 6082 to bypass FSIA would contradict FSIA’s text and structure and improperly infer an abrogation of foreign sovereign immunity where Congress did not clearly provide one.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole and exclusive” basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, so a plaintiff must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception before a federal court may proceed. Verlinden holds that the FSIA comprehensively regulates amenability to suit and “must be applied” in every action against a foreign sovereign, and Amerada Hess confirms that § 1330 displaces other jurisdictional grants such as § 1331. Title III of the Helms-Burton Act, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, authorizes a cause of action against persons who “traffic,” but it nowhere clearly abrogates sovereign immunity or amends the FSIA’s jurisdictional rule, and we do not infer such a displacement from general remedial language. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would create serious practical and diplomatic consequences by opening U.S. courts to suits against foreign state entities without the clear statement Congress ordinarily provides when it withdraws immunity.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FSIA supplies the exclusive basis for jurisdiction over foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities, so a Title III plaintiff must plead and prove a statutory exception to immunity unless Congress clearly abrogated immunity, which Title III does not do on its face. In Helmerich & Payne, the Court reaffirmed FSIA’s centrality and required a legally valid, nonfrivolous showing that an FSIA exception applies before haling a sovereign into U.S. court, reflecting the statute’s careful calibration of international-law and foreign-relations concerns. Reading 22 U.S.C. § 6082 to bypass 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1605 would silently undo Congress’s chosen limits (including nexus requirements) without the unmistakable clarity the Court demands when altering sovereign immunity. While Title III aims to provide remedies for victims of expropriation, fairness and access to justice do not permit courts to create jurisdiction where Congress has not clearly displaced FSIA’s presumption of immunity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The FSIA “provides the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in the courts of this country,” so absent an enumerated FSIA exception, federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction over claims against a foreign state or its agencies/instrumentalities. See Republic of Argentina v. Weltover, Inc., 504 U.S. 607, 611 (1992); OBB Personenverkehr AG v. Sachs, 577 U.S. 27, 30 (2015); Republic of Hungary v. Simon, 604 U.S. 115, 121 (2025). Title III, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, creates a cause of action against persons who “traffic,” but it does not speak with the clarity needed to displace FSIA immunity or create an additional, freestanding jurisdictional grant overriding 28 U.S.C. §§ 1602–1611. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would undermine the statutory coherence and workability of Congress’s comprehensive immunity framework, so plaintiffs must still plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” and its agencies or instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so a plaintiff must plead and prove a statutory exception to immunity to invoke 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a). Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp. holds that FSIA’s comprehensive scheme displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) absent a clear congressional statement overriding immunity, and Title III of Helms-Burton, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, contains no unmistakable abrogation of FSIA immunity. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would impermissibly rewrite the immunity framework Congress enacted in §§ 1602–1611 and would relax a separation-of-powers line Congress itself drew by making immunity the rule and exceptions the only path to jurisdiction. Whatever Title III’s policy aims, they must be pursued through the text Congress adopted—meaning Title III claims against Cuban state entities may proceed only if an FSIA exception applies.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for obtaining subject-matter jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities in U.S. courts, and a plaintiff must plead and prove a statutory FSIA exception to overcome the presumption of immunity. Verlinden and Amerada Hess make clear that § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) and that courts should not infer an implied carve-out from FSIA’s comprehensive scheme absent a clear statement from Congress. Title III of the Helms-Burton Act creates a cause of action for “trafficking,” but it does not unmistakably and expressly abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or amend 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605 to authorize jurisdiction over Cuban state entities without an FSIA exception. Respect for precedent, workability, and the foreign-relations sensitivity of sovereign-immunity rules counsel against reading Title III to bypass FSIA’s framework.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: FSIA provides the “sole and exclusive standards” for jurisdiction and immunity in any suit against a foreign state or its agencies and instrumentalities, so Title III claims may proceed only if the plaintiff pleads and proves a statutory FSIA exception. Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria and Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess make clear that 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants (including § 1331) and that subject-matter jurisdiction “depends on the existence of one of the specified exceptions.” Title III, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, authorizes a cause of action against those who “traffic,” but it does not clearly and explicitly abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or amend FSIA’s comprehensive scheme, and under a textualist reading that silence is insufficient to override FSIA’s presumption of immunity. Harmonizing the statutes therefore requires enforcing Title III against immune defendants only where an FSIA exception applies, rather than treating Title III as an implied carve-out from FSIA.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FSIA supplies the “sole basis” for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, so a plaintiff must plead and prove an applicable FSIA exception to proceed. This Court has repeatedly reaffirmed that exclusivity—most notably in Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434–37 (1989), and again in Saudi Arabia v. Nelson, 507 U.S. 349, 355 (1993)—and Congress must speak clearly if it intends to displace FSIA immunity. Title III of the Helms-Burton Act, 22 U.S.C. § 6082, creates a cause of action but is silent as to waiver/abrogation of sovereign immunity, and a cause of action cannot itself establish jurisdiction or immunity waiver absent a clear statement. Given the procedural-fairness and rule-of-law interests at stake in subjecting foreign sovereign instrumentalities to U.S. litigation, I would require strict FSIA compliance rather than infer an implied carveout that Congress did not expressly enact.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act creates a cause of action against Cuban state agencies and instrumentalities that is independently jurisdiction-conferring (i.e., allows suit without satisfying an exception to immunity under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act).
case_analysis.legal_provision: Title III of the Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 (Helms‑Burton Act), 22 U.S.C. § 6082 et seq., in interaction with the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Exxon Mobil argues that Congress enacted Title III specifically to provide an effective U.S. damages remedy for victims of Cuba’s Castro-era confiscations and for subsequent ‘trafficking’ in that expropriated property, including when trafficking is carried out by Cuban state-owned entities. Exxon (supported by the United States as amicus and business amici) contends that requiring Title III plaintiffs to separately establish a FSIA exception would largely defeat Title III’s remedial purpose because the likely relevant FSIA exceptions are difficult to satisfy on the facts typical of Cuba-expropriation cases. Exxon therefore maintains Title III should be read to permit suits against Cuban agencies/instrumentalities without an additional FSIA exception showing (either because Title III itself displaces FSIA immunity for these claims, or because Title III supplies the necessary jurisdictional authorization).
case_analysis.respondent_position: CIMEX and the other respondents argue that FSIA is the exclusive gateway to jurisdiction over foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, creating a presumption of immunity unless a statutory FSIA exception applies. They contend Title III creates a substantive cause of action against ‘traffickers’ but does not clearly and unequivocally abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or override FSIA’s jurisdictional scheme. Respondents (supported by foreign sovereign immunity and international-law scholar amici) emphasize that reading Title III to bypass FSIA would be inconsistent with FSIA’s exclusivity, would create significant foreign-relations friction, and would contradict the principle that any immunity abrogation must be unmistakably clear in statutory text.
key_precedents: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act framework (general principle of presumptive immunity and exception-based jurisdiction)
Act of State doctrine (as referenced in comparative/international-law discussion in amici materials about indirect impleading and sovereign acts)

John Roberts.reasoning: Petitioners’ best argument is that Title III’s liability for any “person” who “traffics” would be frustrated if Cuban state instrumentalities can claim immunity, but under Amerada Hess and Verlinden we require an unmistakably clear statement before treating a later statute as displacing FSIA’s comprehensive immunity-and-jurisdiction framework. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on FSIA as the “sole basis” for jurisdiction, reinforced by Weltover’s treatment of § 1330(a) as channeling suits against foreign states through FSIA, confirms that a cause of action cannot do the work of an immunity abrogation by implication. Justice Sotomayor is right to note that plaintiffs may still proceed where an FSIA exception applies, which allows a narrow holding: Title III creates substantive liability, but it neither abrogates immunity nor confers jurisdiction independent of FSIA. That approach respects precedent, avoids inferring major foreign-relations consequences from silence, and leaves any Cuba-specific override to Congress to state explicitly.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Petitioners’ best argument is that Title III’s use of “any person” who “traffics” necessarily includes foreign sovereign instrumentalities, but that reading mistakes a substantive cause of action for an unmistakably clear abrogation of immunity. As Chief Justice Roberts explains, Amerada Hess and Verlinden treat FSIA and § 1330(a) as the sole and exclusive gateway to jurisdiction over foreign states, and Title III does not amend §§ 1604–1605 or even mention sovereign immunity. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Weltover reinforces the textual point that other statutes creating liability do not themselves supply jurisdiction or displace FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Under an original public meaning approach, Congress must speak clearly when it means to override immunity in this sensitive domain, and § 6082 does not do so.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioners’ best argument is that Title III’s creation of liability for any “person” who “traffics” in confiscated property would be hollow if Cuban state entities could invoke immunity, but that is a purposive inference that cannot satisfy our clear-statement rule for displacing FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts is right to frame this as a cause-of-action versus jurisdiction/immunity question: under Amerada Hess and Verlinden, FSIA and § 1330(a) supply the “sole and exclusive” route, and Title III nowhere unmistakably abrogates immunity or amends §§ 1604–1605. Justice Kavanaugh’s practical-consequences point further confirms that we should not infer a major foreign-relations shift from statutory silence, particularly where Congress knows how to speak clearly when it wants to strip immunity. So plaintiffs must proceed, if at all, by fitting within an FSIA exception; Title III does not itself provide an end-run around FSIA.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest point remains that Title III’s remedial design—to deter “trafficking” in confiscated property—would be substantially frustrated if Cuban state instrumentalities can invoke FSIA, but that purpose cannot substitute for the clear statement our cases require to displace FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Verlinden is persuasive under my pragmatic approach because it preserves a predictable jurisdictional framework in a sensitive foreign-relations domain and avoids courts creating major international consequences from statutory silence. Justice Kavanaugh’s emphasis on reciprocity and stability reinforces why we should insist on unmistakable textual direction before treating Title III’s cause of action as an immunity abrogation rather than leaving plaintiffs to proceed, where available, under an FSIA exception. I remain attentive to access-to-justice concerns for victims, but the proper path is through FSIA’s exceptions (if satisfied), not an implied Title III end-run around immunity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioners’ best argument—that Title III’s cause of action against any “person” who “traffics” must include foreign sovereign instrumentalities—still fails because it asks us to treat a liability-creating provision as an implied abrogation of immunity without the “unmistakably clear” signal our FSIA cases demand. Chief Justice Roberts is right that Amerada Hess and Verlinden frame FSIA (via §§ 1330 and 1604) as the comprehensive, exclusive gateway for both immunity and jurisdiction, and Title III neither amends FSIA nor speaks to immunity at all. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Weltover underscores that we do not permit end-runs around § 1330(a) through other statutes that create causes of action but lack a clear jurisdictional/immunity override. On a pragmatic textualist view, channeling Title III claims through existing FSIA exceptions preserves statutory coherence and workability while leaving any Cuba-specific immunity abrogation to Congress to state explicitly.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioners’ strongest contention—that Title III would be largely self-defeating if Cuban state entities can invoke immunity—cannot supply the “unmistakably clear” textual statement needed to displace FSIA’s comprehensive scheme. Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow approach is right: § 6082 creates a cause of action, but it neither amends 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604–1605 nor furnishes jurisdiction independent of § 1330(a), and Amerada Hess/Verlinden foreclose treating silence as abrogation. Justice Kavanaugh’s reliance on Weltover underscores that we do not permit statutory end-runs around FSIA by pointing to liability-creating provisions untethered to a clear immunity override. Under a separation-of-powers, textualist method, any Cuba-specific abrogation with serious foreign-relations consequences must come from Congress in clear terms, not judicial inference from purpose.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains that Title III’s liability for any “trafficker” would be significantly narrowed if Cuban state instrumentalities can invoke FSIA, but as Chief Justice Roberts stresses, Amerada Hess and Verlinden require an unmistakably clear statement before treating a later statute as displacing FSIA’s comprehensive immunity-and-jurisdiction scheme. Justice Barrett’s structural point is important: § 1330(a) channels suits against foreign states through FSIA exceptions, and Title III neither amends § 1330/§ 1604 nor even mentions sovereign immunity—so it supplies a cause of action, not an immunity abrogation or independent jurisdictional grant. The opposing side’s purposive argument cannot overcome the clear-statement rule in this foreign-relations domain, and reading an implied override would destabilize the settled FSIA framework with serious reciprocity consequences. No colleague has identified a precedent that meaningfully weakens the “sole basis” line of cases, so my vote remains for Respondent.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The strongest petitioner contention would be that Title III’s creation of liability for “traffickers” necessarily reaches foreign sovereign entities that commercially exploit confiscated property, but under our clear-statement cases and the FSIA’s structure that inference cannot do the work of abrogation. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the FSIA supplies the “sole and exclusive standards” for jurisdiction and immunity, and nothing in 22 U.S.C. § 6082 unmistakably overrides 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330(a) and 1604 or amends the FSIA exceptions. Justice Kavanaugh’s point about preserving the settled, workable FSIA gatekeeping framework reinforces that a cause of action alone cannot create jurisdiction against a “foreign state” absent an applicable FSIA exception. I therefore see no textual basis to treat Title III as an independent jurisdictional grant displacing FSIA, and my vote remains for Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest point remains that Title III’s broad liability for any “trafficker” would be substantially weakened if Cuban state instrumentalities can invoke FSIA, but that policy concern cannot substitute for the unmistakably clear statement our cases require before treating another statute as displacing FSIA’s comprehensive immunity-and-jurisdiction framework. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on Amerada Hess and Verlinden underscores that FSIA is the exclusive gateway for jurisdiction over a foreign state, and Justice Kavanaugh’s emphasis—grounded in Weltover—that a cause of action is not a jurisdictional or immunity override reinforces that Title III’s silence is dispositive. From a progressive pragmatic standpoint, the practical consequences cut both ways: implying abrogation would create serious foreign-relations and reciprocity risks and invite unpredictable, procedurally unfair jurisdictional litigation untethered from FSIA’s structured exceptions. Absent clear congressional direction, plaintiffs must proceed, if at all, by identifying an applicable FSIA exception rather than treating Title III as an implied end-run around sovereign immunity.

John Roberts.reasoning: The FSIA provides the “sole and exclusive standards” for both immunity and subject-matter jurisdiction in civil actions against foreign states and their agencies and instrumentalities, and § 1330(a) displaces other jurisdictional grants. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 437 (1989); Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488, 493 (1983). Title III creates a substantive cause of action against “traffickers,” but it does not speak with the unmistakable clarity required to abrogate sovereign immunity or override FSIA’s comprehensive scheme, especially in light of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1604 and 1330. A narrow, precedent-respecting ruling preserves institutional legitimacy and leaves any immunity-abrogating expansion to Congress in clearer terms.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA provides the exclusive jurisdictional path for suits against a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities unless Congress unmistakably provides otherwise. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428 (1989), describes FSIA as the “sole basis” for such jurisdiction, and nothing in Title III’s text (22 U.S.C. § 6082) clearly displaces FSIA’s immunity rule or supplies an independent jurisdictional grant overriding 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604. A cause of action against “traffickers” is not, by itself, a clear abrogation of sovereign immunity; under a textualist reading, any departure from FSIA’s comprehensive scheme must be explicit in statutory language, not inferred from remedial purpose. Absent a satisfied FSIA exception in §§ 1605–1607, the courts lack jurisdiction over respondents.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The FSIA provides the exclusive, comprehensive scheme for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities in federal court, and we have repeatedly described it as the “sole basis” for such jurisdiction. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434 (1989); see also 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604. Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a cause of action against “traffickers,” but it does not contain the unmistakably clear text needed to displace FSIA’s immunity rule or to create an independent jurisdiction-conferring pathway for suits against Cuban state entities, particularly given the foreign-relations consequences of implied abrogation. Whatever Title III’s remedial purpose, it cannot override the FSIA’s presumption of immunity absent a clear statutory statement, and plaintiffs therefore must satisfy an applicable FSIA exception to proceed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in federal court,” and courts may exercise jurisdiction over a foreign state or its agencies/instrumentalities only if an FSIA exception applies. Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 439 (1989); see also Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488–89 (1983). Title III of Helms‑Burton creates a substantive cause of action against “traffickers,” but it does not speak with the unmistakable clarity needed to displace FSIA’s immunity-and-exception framework or to create an independent jurisdictional grant overriding 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611. Given the serious foreign-relations consequences of reading Title III to bypass FSIA and the statutory presumption of immunity for foreign sovereigns, I would require plaintiffs to proceed through an established FSIA exception rather than infer a Cuba-specific abrogation from remedial purpose alone.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: FSIA provides the "sole basis" for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state and its agencies/instrumentalities in U.S. courts, so absent a FSIA exception a federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction. See Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488 (1983); Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 443 (1989); 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604. Title III (22 U.S.C. § 6082) creates a substantive cause of action against "traffickers," but it does not speak with the unmistakable clarity needed to displace FSIA’s immunity-and-exceptions scheme or to confer jurisdiction independently. Reading Title III to bypass FSIA would conflict with Congress’s comprehensive framework in FSIA and invites serious workability and foreign-relations problems better avoided absent a clear textual instruction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the exclusive jurisdictional framework for suits against foreign states and their agencies or instrumentalities, and we have repeatedly described it as “the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in federal court.” Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 434, 438–39 (1989). Title III of the Helms–Burton Act creates a substantive cause of action against those who “traffic” in confiscated property, but it does not speak with the “unmistakably clear” specificity needed to displace FSIA’s immunity-and-exceptions scheme or to confer jurisdiction independent of 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604–1605. Respecting the separation of powers and Congress’s chosen jurisdictional gatekeeping, courts may not infer an abrogation of foreign sovereign immunity from broad remedial purpose where the statutory text does not clearly override FSIA.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The FSIA supplies the exclusive basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over suits against a foreign state and its agencies or instrumentalities, and immunity presumptively applies unless a statutory FSIA exception is satisfied. This Court has repeatedly held that the FSIA “provides the sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction” in such cases, including in Republic of Argentina v. Weltover, 504 U.S. 607, 610–11 (1992), and Amerada Hess, 488 U.S. at 437, which rejected reliance on other jurisdictional grants like § 1331. Title III of the Helms‑Burton Act creates a substantive cause of action against “traffickers,” but it does not contain the unmistakably clear text required to abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or to displace the FSIA’s comprehensive scheme, so courts must still find jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) and an applicable FSIA exception. Practical and institutional considerations reinforce that reading, because bypassing FSIA would invite foreign-relations friction and undermine the settled, workable jurisdictional framework Congress enacted in the FSIA.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Textually, the FSIA supplies the exclusive basis for subject-matter jurisdiction over a “foreign state” and its “agenc[ies] or instrumentalit[ies],” allowing suit only when a statutory exception applies. 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330(a), 1603(a)–(b), 1604. Our precedents emphasize that comprehensiveness: § 1330 “sets forth the sole and exclusive standards” for immunity and jurisdiction, displacing other jurisdictional routes unless Congress unmistakably provides otherwise. Verlinden B.V. v. Central Bank of Nigeria, 461 U.S. 480, 488, 493 (1983); Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp., 488 U.S. 428, 435 & n.3, 437 (1989). Title III creates a substantive cause of action against “traffick[ers],” 22 U.S.C. § 6082, but it does not clearly and unequivocally abrogate foreign sovereign immunity or amend FSIA’s jurisdictional scheme; absent such unmistakable clarity, FSIA immunity remains and plaintiffs must satisfy an FSIA exception.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: FSIA supplies the “sole basis for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state” and its agencies/instrumentalities, so absent a clearly applicable FSIA exception a federal court lacks subject-matter jurisdiction. Title III (22 U.S.C. § 6082) creates a cause of action against “traffickers,” but it does not contain an unmistakably clear statement displacing FSIA’s immunity-and-exception framework or independently conferring jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604. Given the serious foreign-relations and reciprocity consequences of implied immunity abrogation—and the procedural-fairness value of clear jurisdictional rules—I would require plaintiffs to satisfy an FSIA exception rather than infer a Title III override.
